structure.title: Travel and recollection
structure.text: Books 1–6 follow displaced Trojans seeking a future home, with earlier events recounted within the journey.

structure.title: Settlement and conflict
structure.text: Books 7–12 shift towards Italy, where a promised future must encounter people with existing homes and obligations.

people.name: Aeneas
people.text: A prince of fallen Troy, carrying his father and his household gods, who has been told by the gods to found a new home in Italy.

people.name: Dido
people.text: The queen of Carthage, herself an exile who has built a new city, who welcomes the shipwrecked Trojans and hears Aeneas tell his story.

people.name: Juno and Venus
people.text: The queen of the gods, who hates the Trojans and works to stop Aeneas, and the goddess of love, his mother, who works to protect him.

context.title: Rome's imagined ancestry
context.text: Know the starting point: the Greeks have sacked Troy after a ten-year siege. Aeneas, a Trojan prince and son of Venus, escapes with his father and son and is fated to found the line that leads to Rome. Virgil wrote under Augustus, whose family claimed descent from that son, Iulus.

context.title: Pietas
context.text: This virtue involves obligations to gods, family, and community. Those obligations can conflict with personal happiness and with one another.
context.takeaway: Duty does not guarantee an easy choice.

notice.text: Attend to those displaced by another person's destiny.
notice.why: The poem lets the cost of founding remain visible.
Repeated separation keeps the journey from becoming a simple ascent to greatness.

opening: Aeneas escapes the destruction of Troy carrying his father and leading his young son. Survival should be enough, but the gods require him to carry a future civilisation as well. He must find a home for his people, even when the places and people he encounters offer reasons to stop travelling. Virgil gives Rome a magnificent origin and lets the losses remain visible inside it: love interrupted, lives spent, and a promised greatness whose beneficiaries have not yet been born.
